arxiv:1701.06538.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer

posts.t: Holding compute near 8 million operations per timestep, a language model kept improving as sparse experts were added: at 65536 experts (68 billion parameters), perplexity on 100 billion words was 39% below a matched baseline. At 131072 it got worse.

cite.quote: test perplexity improves significantly up to 65536 experts (68 billion parameters), dropping 39% lower than the computationally matched baseline, but degrades at 131072 experts

posts.t: On the 1-billion-word benchmark at equal compute, 4096 experts gave 24% lower test perplexity, and the fastest 4-billion-parameter MoE beat the best published LSTM (at equal epochs) with 6% of its computation. WMT'14 BLEU rose 1.34 (En→Fr) and 1.12 (En→De) over GNMT baselines.

cite.quote: beats the best published result (when controlling for the number of training epochs), despite requiring only 6% of the computation

posts.t: How: up to thousands of feed-forward experts sit between LSTM layers. A gate adds tunable noise, keeps the top k scores (4 experts per input in the language models) and zeroes the rest. Extra losses keep experts evenly used; sharding keeps their batches large.

cite.quote: Before taking the softmax function, we add tunable Gaussian noise, then keep only the top k values, setting the rest to -∞

posts.t: Figure 3 (numbers in Table 8): test perplexity against parameters at fixed compute. After 100 billion words it falls from 47.0 for the dense LSTM baseline to 28.9 at 68 billion parameters, then rises to 29.2 at 137 billion. After 10 billion words the curve bottoms out at 38.2.

cite.quote: Figure 3 shows test perplexity as a function of capacity after training on 10 billion words (top line) and 100 billion words (bottom line).

posts.t: What it changes: parameters and compute per token become separate dials, and extra parameters pay most when data is plentiful. On 1 billion words, returns seemed to diminish past 1 billion MoE parameters; on the larger corpus, gains continued much further.

cite.quote: The widening gap between the two lines demonstrates (unsurprisingly) that increased model capacity helps more on larger training sets.

posts.t: Caveat: the fixed compute is counted in multiply-adds per timestep, not hardware. The low-compute MoE models ran at 0.74–0.90 TFLOPS/GPU against 1.07–1.29 for dense baselines, the largest at 0.30, and the two biggest needed 64 and 128 GPUs to hold their parameters.

cite.quote: For our low-computation MoE models, computation efficiency ranged from 0.74-0.90 TFLOPS/GPU

posts.t: Read it if you build sparse models: §2–4 (pp. 3–6) for noisy top-k gating, the shrinking-batch fix and the balancing losses; §5 (pp. 6–9) for results. Appendix D (p. 16) adds a memory trick: Adam with β1 = 0 and a factored second moment.

cite.quote: To reduce the size of the second moment estimator, we replace it with a factored approximation.

posts.t: With no clipping or KL penalty, several epochs of updates per batch on the probability-ratio surrogate averaged −0.39 on 7 MuJoCo tasks, below a random policy's 0, because of one task. Clipping the ratio to 1 ± 0.2 scored 0.82, where 1 is the best result.

cite.quote: the score is negative for the setting without clipping or penalties, because for one environment (half cheetah) it leads to a very negative score

posts.t: The best clipping settings beat every adaptive and fixed KL-penalty setting tried, and PPO beat tuned TRPO, CEM and A2C variants on almost all continuous-control tasks. Of 49 Atari games it won 30 on reward over all of training, to ACER's 18; ACER won 28 on final reward, PPO 19.

cite.quote: We see that PPO outperforms the previous methods on almost all the continuous control environments.

posts.t: How: the loss takes the minimum of ratio × advantage and its clipped version, a pessimistic bound: changes in the ratio count when they make the objective worse, not when they improve it. N actors gather T steps; then K epochs of minibatch Adam. MuJoCo: T = 2048, 10 epochs.

cite.quote: we only ignore the change in probability ratio when it would make the objective improve, and we include it when it makes the objective worse

posts.t: Figure 1: one term of the clipped objective against the probability ratio r. With a positive advantage it rises with r and goes flat past 1 + ε; with a negative advantage it is flat below 1 − ε. Starting from r = 1 (red dot), an update gains nothing by leaving the interval.

cite.quote: for positive advantages (left) and negative advantages (right). The red circle on each plot shows the starting point for the optimization

posts.t: What it changes: TRPO-like stability without second-order optimization. The authors say PPO needs only a few lines of code change to a vanilla policy gradient implementation, and unlike TRPO it applies when the policy and value function share parameters.

cite.quote: requiring only few lines of code change to a vanilla policy gradient implementation

posts.t: Caveat: the objective comparison is 3 seeds on each of 7 tasks, one million timesteps each, with no error bars, and ε was searched on the same benchmark that scores it. The margins are modest: 0.82 for the best clipping setting against 0.74 for the best adaptive KL penalty.

cite.quote: Each algorithm was run on all 7 environments, with 3 random seeds on each.

posts.t: Read it if you use or tune PPO: §3 (p. 3) defines the clipped objective in a page, Table 1 (p. 6) is the ablation, and Appendix A (p. 10) lists the hyperparameters most implementations copy. The humanoid showcase (§6.3) and the 49-game curves can be skipped.

cite.quote: Our experiments compare the performance of various different versions of the surrogate objective, and find that the version with the clipped probability ratios performs best.

openai:gpt1.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training

posts.t: One task-agnostic Transformer, pre-trained as a language model on over 7,000 unpublished books and fine-tuned with little more than a linear output layer, beat architectures built for each task on 9 of 12 datasets, Story Cloze by 8.9% absolute.

cite.quote: Our general task-agnostic model outperforms discriminatively trained models that employ architectures specifically crafted for each task

posts.t: Overall GLUE score 72.8 against a previous best of 68.9; on CoLA, grammatical acceptability, 45.4 against 35.0; RACE up 5.7% and MultiNLI up 1.5% absolute. Each pre-trained layer transferred helped, up to 9% on MultiNLI with full transfer.

cite.quote: We also achieve an overall score of 72.8 on the GLUE benchmark, which is significantly better than the previous best of 68.9.

posts.t: How: a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer (768-dimensional states, 12 heads) trained as a language model on BooksCorpus, chosen for its long contiguous text. Fine-tuning flattens structured inputs, like premise and hypothesis, into one token sequence with delimiters.

cite.quote: We trained a 12-layer decoder-only transformer with masked self-attention heads (768 dimensional states and 12 attention heads).

posts.t: Figure 2, right: zero-shot scores, scaled from random (0) to state of the art (1). For sentiment the model appends 'very' and compares the probabilities of positive and negative. Over pre-training, sentiment rises to about 0.68, QA to about 0.26. Values read off the chart.

cite.quote: Plot showing the evolution of zero-shot performance on different tasks as a function of LM pre-training updates.

posts.t: What it changes: pre-train once and fine-tune with minimal changes, instead of designing an architecture per task. Without pre-training the same Transformer scored 14.8% lower across tasks; a 2048-unit LSTM in its place lost 5.6 points of average score.

cite.quote: We observe that the lack of pre-training hurts performance across all the tasks, resulting in a 14.8% decrease compared to our full model.

posts.t: Caveat: it trailed on 3 of 12 datasets, among them RTE, with 2490 examples, at 56% against 61.7% for a multi-task biLSTM. The authors think multi-task training would likely help but did not test it, and each result is a single number without error bars.

cite.quote: we achieve an accuracy of 56%, which is below the 61.7% reported by a multi-task biLSTM model

posts.t: Read it if you train or study pre-trained language models: §3.3 with Figure 1 (p. 4) for turning structured inputs into one sequence, and §5 (pp. 7–8) for layer transfer, zero-shot behavior and ablations. §2 is related work; the results tables in §4 can be skimmed.

cite.quote: we use a traversal-style approach [52], where we convert structured inputs into an ordered sequence that our pre-trained model can process

bstj:30-1-50.title: Prediction and Entropy of Printed English

posts.t: Shannon measured English by having a person guess text letter by letter. With up to 100 letters of context, the guesses suggest an entropy of the order of one bit per letter, a redundancy of roughly 75%; 26 equally likely letters carry 4.7 bits.

cite.quote: the long range statistical effects (up to 100 letters) reduce the entropy to something of the order of one bit per letter

posts.t: In one passage, a subject guessed 89 of 129 letters (69%) right. Allowed to keep guessing, another run got 79 of 102 symbols on the first try and only eight needed more than five. Guessing the preceding letter instead felt much harder, but scores were only slightly poorer.

cite.quote: Out of 102 symbols the subject guessed right on the first guess 79 times

posts.t: How: the sequence of guess numbers is a reversible encoding of the text, so it has the same entropy. From how often the first, second and later guesses were right, Shannon proves upper and lower bounds on the N-gram entropy, using a hundred 15-letter samples from one book.

cite.quote: One hundred samples of English text were selected at random from a book, each fifteen letters in length.

posts.t: Fig. 4 (p. 63): the upper and lower bounds against letters of context, plotted from the table on p. 64. The upper bound starts at 4.03 bits with no letter known; both fall fast, then level off amid sampling noise, reaching 1.3 and .6 at 100 letters.

cite.quote: Upper and lower experimental bounds for the entropy of 27-letter English.

posts.t: What it changes: prediction and compression become one problem. A text can be sent as its reduced form, the guess numbers, between two identical prediction devices, and ideal prediction concentrates probability more than any other reversible translation of the same reach.

cite.quote: In fact, a communication system could be constructed in which only the reduced text is transmitted from one point to the other.

posts.t: Caveat: the bounds come from human guesses on small samples, with 'still considerable sampling error'. The lower bound is proved only for an ideal predictor; Shannon argues from 'Some rough calculations' that this more than offsets humans guessing imperfectly.

cite.quote: Some rough calculations, however, indicate that the discrepancy between the actual FN and the lower bound with ideal prediction

posts.t: Read it if you think about language models as predictors: §3 (pp. 54–58) for the guessing experiments and the reduced-text idea, §6 (p. 64) for the bounds. §2 (pp. 51–54) gives N-gram estimates from frequency tables; §4–5 (pp. 58–63) are proofs to skim.

cite.quote: the reduced text can be considered to be an encoded form of the original, the result of passing the original text through a reversible transducer

posts.t: Chinchilla 70B, trained mostly on text and used with arithmetic coding as a lossless compressor, beat PNG on grayscale ImageNet patches and FLAC on speech, provided the model's own size is not counted. It beat every classical compressor tested, on text too.

cite.quote: language models, while trained primarily on text, also appear to be general-purpose compressors, as they outperform all other compressors, even on image and audio data

posts.t: Compressed over raw size: the abstract gives Chinchilla 70B 43.4% on ImageNet patches and 16.4% on LibriSpeech, against PNG's 58.5% and FLAC's 30.3%; Table 1 gives the model 48.0% and 21.0%. On enwik9 text it reached 8.3%, against 23.0% for LZMA2 on the whole file.

cite.quote: Chinchilla 70B achieves compression rates of 43.4% on ImageNet patches and 16.4% on LibriSpeech samples, beating domain-specific compressors like PNG (58.5%) or FLAC (30.3%), respectively

posts.t: How: arithmetic coding turns next-symbol probabilities into a code of about −log2 p bits per symbol, so minimizing log loss minimizes compressed size. Each 1GB dataset was cut into 2048-byte chunks compressed separately: images as grayscale 32×64 patches, audio as 1-byte samples.

cite.quote: minimizing the log -loss is equivalent to minimizing the compression rate of that model used as a lossless compressor with arithmetic coding

posts.t: Figure 2, log-log: adjusted rate, model size included, against model size for Transformers trained on enwik8. enwik8 and enwik9 dip, then climb; enwik7 only climbs, steeply past about 10^6 bytes. On enwik9, the largest set, it stays low to about 10^7. Values read off the chart.

cite.quote: The larger the dataset, the more parameters we can afford.

posts.t: What it changes: tokenization is a pre-compression, not a free gain. On enwik9, a 38M Transformer reached 6.4% on raw ASCII bytes and 9.0% with a 20K-token BPE vocabulary; only the 200K model gained, to 19.3% at 20K tokens from 22.9%. Larger vocabularies do fit more in context.

cite.quote: for bigger models, it seems that the converse happens: having a larger token vocabulary harms the final compression rate of the model

posts.t: Caveat: count the model, at 2 bytes per parameter, and Chinchilla 70B's adjusted rate on the 1GB ImageNet set is 14048.0%, against gzip's 70.7%. The authors say a foundation model compresses non-trivially, net of its size, only on datasets in the order of TBs.

cite.quote: a foundation model can only achieve non-trivial (adjusted) compression rates when evaluated on datasets in the order of TBs (or more)

posts.t: Read it if you think about what pretraining learns or how far to scale: §2 (pp. 3–4) states the prediction–compression equivalence; §3.2–3.3 (pp. 5–7) has Table 1 and the model-size trade-off; §3.6 (p. 8) tokenization. Appendix A works the coding example by hand.

cite.quote: larger models achieve better compression rates on larger datasets, justifying recent trends in model scaling

posts.t: These notes rate 17 reasoning processes, from peer review and prediction markets to LLM judges, on cost to run and cost to corrupt. By the authors' rough judgments, nothing yet is both cheap to run and hard to corrupt; they call that a conjecture to test.

cite.quote: Plotting the catalogue’s 17 processes on those two axes leaves one corner empty: nothing yet is both cheap to run and hard to corrupt.

posts.t: The proposed way in is deterrence: bonds, clawbacks and occasional audits raise the cost to corrupt while adding little to the cost to run, so it 'looks like the most promising route into the corner'. Hardening by verification raises both costs. Neither move has been measured.

cite.quote: Deterrence (bonds, clawbacks, occasional audits) raises the cost to corrupt while adding little to the cost to run

posts.t: The map (fig0): processes placed by cost to run and cost to corrupt, shaped by family. AI-native ones cluster at the cheap, easy-to-corrupt end, resolution-grounded ones toward expensive and hard to corrupt. Two arrows from the single LLM judge show verification and deterrence.

cite.quote: Shapes are the catalogue’s three families: grounded in resolution or track records, institutional judgment, AI-native.

posts.t: Caveat: the site calls itself 'drafts and conjectures rather than settled results'. The positions are the authors' own rough judgments, and several chapters, such as certification, the market for truth, and law and liability, are only planned.

cite.quote: This is an early research exploration, with drafts and conjectures rather than settled results.

posts.t: Read it if you want the site's map: start with Chapter 1 and 'Cruxes', then The Process Catalogue for the ratings. 'LLM Epistemics in Production' reports QURI's own failures, and every formalism is graded [exact], [standard shape] or [heuristic].

cite.quote: Formalisms are graded [exact], [standard shape] or [heuristic], by how far each can be trusted.

posts.t: In this wiki's coding of 154 rated evaluation systems, those paid anything by the party they rate had an established failure in 27 of 67 cases, against 10 of 62 paid nothing: an odds ratio of 3.5 (90% interval 1.6–7.8). Who mainly funds them says little.

cite.quote: Where the rated party pays anything, 27 of 67 failed, against 10 of 62 where it pays nothing

posts.t: The wiki's bet: we know how to do one careful evaluation of a grant or charity; the hard part is the ten-thousandth, cheap and reliable enough to be used. Its core pattern: a cheap layer scores every item, and a hidden random sample also goes to a trusted evaluator to measure it.

cite.quote: a hidden random sample also goes to an expensive, trusted evaluator, and that sample measures how far the cheap layer can be trusted

posts.t: Chart (fig0): share with an established failure, 27% across all 154. By main funder: the rated party 12 of 35, mixed 11 of 39, a third party 9 of 35, public money 4 of 19, users 5 of 26. By payment from the rated party: none, 10 of 62; on the side, 15 of 32.

cite.quote: Share of 154 rated systems with an established failure: one found by a regulator, court, audit or named investigation.

posts.t: What it changes: when judging a rating, review or certification system, ask whether the rated party pays the evaluator anything at all, through fees, advertising or logo licences, not only who its main funder is.

cite.quote: What does matter is whether the rated party pays it anything at all, through fees, advertising or logo licences

posts.t: Caveat: funding was coded from public sources by one coder, a failure counts only if a regulator, court, audit or named investigation found it, and finding none is not the same as not failing. The side-payment rows leave out 25 systems whose side payments were not checked.

cite.quote: The lower three rows leave out 25 systems whose side payments were not checked.

posts.t: Read it if you design grant review, charity assessment or research triage at scale: Chapter 1, the worked example (1,000 grants a year, four designs), then 'Evaluation Systems in the Wild' for the coding. The pages are working notes, drafted largely with Claude Code.

cite.quote: a funder reviewing 1,000 grants a year under four designs, with illustrative costs

posts.t: QURI's deployed LLM tools, read as oversight evidence: checks cheap enough to run on every draft aren't yet trustworthy enough to gate anything. RoastMyPost flags errors with a 'significant' false-positive rate, so it is pitched for drafts, not gatekeeping.

cite.quote: the judge-grounded verdicts cheap enough to run on every draft are not yet trustworthy enough to gate anything downstream

posts.t: Squiggle AI: 168 workflows from 30 external users at $0.10–0.35 each; its developer reports his model-building time falling from 2–3 hours to 10–30 minutes. Its estimates came out 'highly overconfident (despite some warnings in the prompts)': the obvious fix did not suffice.

cite.quote: the obvious mitigation was tried and did not suffice

posts.t: The $300 Fermi competition used Claude 3.5 Sonnet as judge, three runs averaged, with 40% of the score for surprise to rationalist and EA readers. Participants caught calculation errors in the AI-coded scoring app, and the recount changed the winner.

cite.quote: the recount raised one entry’s Surprise score enough to change the winner

posts.t: What it changes: budget for upkeep and false positives, not just setup. 'Prompt engineering is a recurring tax, not a setup cost'; a critic that cries wolf hands verification back to the human; and under tight budgets, chunked pipelines beat agentic loops.

cite.quote: Prompt engineering is a recurring tax, not a setup cost.

posts.t: Caveat: this is QURI grading QURI. The page is synthesized from QURI's own write-ups, none is a controlled experiment, and no calibration, accuracy or per-evaluator precision numbers have been published; the false-positive rate is a qualitative self-assessment.

cite.quote: no formal calibration, accuracy, or per-evaluator precision evaluation of any of these systems has been published

posts.t: Read it if you build LLM evaluators: the Fermi section shows why surprise without validation 'pays for persuasion as readily as truth'; 'What production teaches that proposals don't' gives four lessons; the open questions ask what false-positive rate makes a critic net-positive.

cite.quote: What false-positive rate makes an automated critic net-positive for a given reader

posts.t: This wiki grades eight evaluation systems on rungs from 'ad hoc' (0) to 'accountable' (5). The most trusted by reputation, peer review and Cochrane, get 1; GRE essay scoring, where a human reads every essay beside the machine, gets the top grade, 4.

cite.quote: The top grade thus goes to a design in which the machine checks a human on every item and saves at most the second read

posts.t: Behind the low marks: a meta-analysis of 48 studies found peer reviewers' mean inter-rater κ ≈ 0.17; NeurIPS's two-committee experiments found about half the accepted list would change on a rerun; four raters using Cochrane's RoB 2 tool on 70 trials reached κ 0.16.

cite.quote: A meta-analysis of 48 studies found mean inter-rater κ ≈ 0.17 (Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel 2010).

posts.t: How: each rung is a test: 1, one written procedure and scale; 2, a stated error with an interval; 3, that error re-measured in operation; 4, error under deliberate gaming; 5, outside audit, disclosed payer, appeal route. The grade is the highest rung passed with all rungs below.

cite.quote: A system’s grade is the highest rung whose test it passes together with every rung below.

posts.t: What it changes: the page argues for borrowing mature standards, educational testing's and ISO/IEC 17025 for labs, not starting from scratch, and never skipping gaming tests when a score gates value: every seriously attacked system was attacked through its score's incentive.

cite.quote: That is the Goodhart pattern, and it is why rung 4 cannot be skipped by anything that gates value.

posts.t: Caveat: eight hand-picked systems, so the page calls its observations hypotheses, and the placements are the wiki's judgments from public documentation, wrong wherever a system measures more internally than it publishes. 'Error' means disagreement with a reference.

cite.quote: The placements are judgments from public documentation and will be wrong wherever a system measures more internally than it publishes.

posts.t: Read it if you run or fund a judgment-based evaluation: the rung table and its tests, then the per-system notes, METR's and the GRE's the most instructive, and 'What the grading suggests'. The open questions ask whether grade predicts documented failure better than funding does.

cite.quote: Grading the 161 catalogue systems would show whether most cluster at 1, and whether grade predicts documented failure better than funding model does.

posts.t: Instead of a 4–20 month forecasting competition, this early QURI idea sketches a paid team of 3–9 full-time equivalents in sprints of 1 to 4 weeks, each a full cycle: write questions, forecast, deliver to clients, check the answers were decision-relevant.

cite.quote: Rather than aiming for a Waterfall model style 4-20 month forecasting competition, the EFTF would work in sprints of 1 to 4 weeks.

posts.t: The diagnosis: much excitement about judgemental forecasting, little implementation. The Good Judgement Project works on year-long, multi-million dollar contracts; GJ Open and Metaculus rely on volunteers, often slow to deliver. Question writing also needs iteration.

cite.quote: There’s currently a lot of excitement around judgemental forecasting but relatively little implementation.

posts.t: How: a proposal, not a result, meant as QURI's main focus for 2–4 years. Small team (~$200K–$500K a year): a manager, 2 full-time forecaster equivalents, a part-time engineer, advisors, assistants. Medium (~$400K–$900K): adds a client lead, data roles and part-time forecasters.

cite.quote: This is proposed for the primary focus of the Quantified Uncertainty Research Institute for the next 2-4 years.

posts.t: What it changes: forecasts become maintained products. In a fictional example, the team checks a nuclear-risk index with its researchers, finds 'nuclear attack' meant different things to different people, and updates forecasts yearly via public APIs feeding other risk models.

cite.quote: This is done using the forecast APIs, meaning that they will continue to be updated as new predictions are made.

posts.t: Caveat: an untested idea. The case for a paid team rests on the author's view that volunteers are unreliable and that question design needs rapid iteration; the author says it is 'not completely clear why' implementation lags, and the one engagement described is fictional.

cite.quote: It’s not completely clear why this is, but it seems like there is a lot of innovation yet to occur.

posts.t: Read it if you are designing a forecasting service or team: the summary, 'Description of need' and the team sizes with costs. 'Comparisons to other services' sets it against engineering consultancies, research teams, superforecasting teams and open tournaments.

cite.quote: The EFTF would be more experimental in technique, follow a compressed workflow, and release their research and process improvement findings to the public.

posts.t: Industry-funded drug and device studies reach favorable conclusions more often (RR 1.34). In this page's model, spin alone weakens such a conclusion but never turns it against the claim. With illustrative inputs it keeps about 44% of its weight.

cite.quote: funding bias can weaken a favorable conclusion toward worthlessness; turning it into evidence against the claim takes a second mechanism, selection on the truth

posts.t: The data, quoted from reviews: for drugs and devices, RR 1.34 (95% CI 1.19–1.51), and funded studies' conclusions match their own results less often (RR 0.83). In nutrition and tobacco, ORs reach 7.6 and 88, but pooled nutrition studies give RR 1.31, not significant.

cite.quote: the effect is modest and tight (RR ~1.3; pooled OR ~3.6); in nutrition and tobacco it is much larger (OR 7–88)

posts.t: How: a funder who makes favorable conclusions k times likelier, whether or not the claim is true, leaves the likelihood ratio unchanged. Spin, reporting unfavorable conclusions as favorable at rate s, pulls it toward 1, never past. Only selection on the truth can flip the sign.

cite.quote: Under any bias applied regardless of the truth, a funded favorable conclusion stays (weak) evidence for H.

posts.t: Chart (fig0): a funded favorable conclusion's likelihood ratio against spin rate s, falling from 4 toward 1, never below. Lundh's estimate sits at s ≈ 0.34, ratio ≈ 1.8. If funders of failing products were twice as likely to produce such a study (illustrative), it is 0.92.

cite.quote: Spin alone weakens a funded favorable conclusion toward worthless but never past it; only selection on the truth can make it count against H.

posts.t: What it changes: discount a sponsored favorable conclusion; invert it only if funders plausibly select on the truth. The discount belongs to the funding arrangement, not the source's character, and the result–conclusion gap is a candidate spin signal that needs no ground truth.

cite.quote: It needs no ground truth, only consistency between a study’s data and its conclusion.

posts.t: Caveat: the 44% assumes the whole effect is spin and uses illustrative inputs (an independent likelihood ratio of 4). The reviews' ratios cannot separate spin from selection, and if sponsors simply fund products likely to work, the conversion overstates spin.

cite.quote: The ratios in the table cannot separate these.

posts.t: Read it if you assess sponsored research: the table and the derivation ('The numbers' and 'From odds ratios to a likelihood-ratio discount') are the core. 'Open questions' lists four next steps, each a measurement.

cite.quote: Is the gap between the tight drug estimates (~1.3×) and the large, wide nutrition/tobacco ones real, or an artifact of sample size and coding latitude?

ia:manualforsolutio00hittrich.title: Manual for the solution of military ciphers

posts.t: In 1916 an Army captain wrote that of the hundreds of real cipher messages he had examined, at least nine-tenths were solved by the methods in this manual. The usual failures were very short messages.

cite.quote: Of the hundreds of actual cipher messages examined by the writer, at least nine-tenths have been solved by the methods to be set forth.
cite.label: vi

posts.t: Why: the amateur 'invents and there is no one to tell him' that his design is centuries old, so amateur ciphers fall into a few easy classes. He traces most modern substitution ciphers to the Abbe Tritheme, 1499, and concludes no message should be considered indecipherable.

cite.quote: he invents and there is no one to tell him that his invention is, in principle, hundreds of years old.
cite.label: vii

posts.t: How, in one line: count letters. If about 40% of an English cipher's letters are vowels and about 30% are L, N, R, S or T, he treats it as a transposition, the letters only rearranged. If these shares do not hold within 5%, it is 'certainly a substitution cipher'.

cite.quote: If these proportions do not hold within 5%, one way or the other, the cipher is certainly a substitution cipher.

posts.t: Table I, p. 6 (k15): letter counts in 10,000 letters of English military orders and reports: E 1277, T 855, O 807, A 778, down to Q 8. Beside them, the counts per 200 letters are printed as rows of 1s, a bar chart set in type. Vowels come to 38.37%.

cite.quote: Vowels AEIOU = 38.37%; consonants LNRST=31.86%

posts.t: What it changes: a key is only as secret as its source. In Hitt's London case, repeats mostly spaced at multiples of 5 pointed to a five-letter key, CHBEF, read as 27145: the sum in the previous day's newspaper notice, 'Will deposit £27 14s 5d tomorrow'.

cite.quote: the key becomes 27145 and we may connect it with the "personal" which appeared in the same paper the day before

posts.t: Caveat: 'nine-tenths' is his own count, over messages made by US Army methods, Mexican armies and their secret agents, and other common methods. The notes cover only simpler ciphers; the hardest substitution ciphers need long messages, and he defers to European authorities.

cite.quote: The methods of analysis given in these notes cover only the simpler varieties of cipher

posts.t: Read it if you like inference from evidence: pp. 5–25 hold the frequency tables and the tests that sort a cipher by class; the London case (pp. 59–63) and Moorman's Playfair method (pp. 78–83) show them at work. Skip pp. 26–30 unless you have a transposition to break.

cite.quote: Lieut. Frank Moorman, U. S. Army, has developed a method for determining the letters which make up the key word in a Playfair cipher.
